phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar [t] plus pure open [a]; Māori t is unaspirated, with none of the puff English puts on 'top.'
The velar nasal [ŋ] — ng as in 'singer,' never as in 'finger' — one sound, though two letters.
Tapped alveolar [ɾ] plus the diphthong [oa] ('long, extensive'); the diphthong draws the stress to this syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tah-ngah-ROH-ah' — say ng as in 'singer,' tap the r, and let the last two vowels glide together.

kin.label: Tahitian
kin.form: Ta'aroa, the self-existent supreme creator of Tahiti (Henry, Ancient Tahiti)

kin.label: Tongan–Samoan
kin.form: Tangaloa, the supreme creator; his messenger the plover Tuli brought up the sand of the first islands (Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology)

kin.label: Hawaiian
kin.form: Kanaloa, god of the deep ocean and the underworld, companion of Kāne (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology)

pronunciation.note: Tangaroa is the Māori continuation of Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa — the same name the Tahitians lengthen into Ta'aroa the creator and the Tongans keep as Tangaloa. No vowel length distinguishes the Māori form, so the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII spelling loses: Tier 2, a display fact only. The ng is not two letters but one sound, the velar nasal English lacks.

domains.title: Tangaroa
domains.subtitle: Ocean
domains.lead: Tangaroa is the sea given will: lord of ocean, fish, and all that swims, son of the Sky Father and Earth Mother, and the brother who fled to the deep when his parents were torn apart. Every fish is his child, every canoe his guest, and every storm over the water is family business.

cards.name: Lord of Ocean
cards.desc: He took the sea for his domain when his parents were separated, vowing in the recitations never to return to the land.

cards.name: Father of Fishes
cards.desc: With Hine-moana, the ocean woman, he is ancestor of every finned and swimming creature the nets take.

cards.name: The Exiled Brother
cards.desc: Tāwhirimātea's war drove him from the coast; his grandchildren scattered to sea and shore, splitting into fish and lizard.

cards.name: One Name, Many Islands
cards.desc: Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Tangaloa in Tonga and Samoa, Kanaloa in Hawai'i — one ocean god under four island names.

symbols.name: The fish-hook (matau)
symbols.meaning: The carved hook with which his descendants take his children from the sea — every catch a petition, every offering a repayment.

symbols.name: The whale and the shark
symbols.meaning: His largest and most feared children; the whale (tohorā) and the shark (mangō) carry his mana in bulk.

symbols.name: The canoe (waka)
symbols.meaning: The vessel that crosses his domain; canoes were tapu and addressed as kin, because the sea is a relative who must be asked.

symbols.name: The tide
symbols.meaning: Tangaroa-whakamau-tai, 'Tangaroa who fixes the tides' — one of his names, and the rhythm by which fishermen read him.

symbols.name: The lizard (ngarara)
symbols.meaning: His grandchildren who hid ashore: the lizards, fish that chose the land — kin, yet forever on the wrong side of the beach.

mythology.lead: Tangaroa's stories are the Māori ocean chapter of the great separation cycle — and then the cycle widens: the same name, in other dialects, becomes the supreme creator of the whole Polynesian triangle. The Māori knew what the comparison would later prove.

myths.title: Born Between the Embrace
myths.text: Tangaroa was born into the darkness that lay between Ranginui, the Sky, and Papatūānuku, the Earth, whose embrace left no room and no light for their children. With his brothers Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike he grew to manhood in that cramped twilight, and with them he debated how to escape: Tūmatauenga counseled killing the parents outright, Tāne proposed forcing them apart. When Tāne at last pushed Ranginui into the sky and light flooded the world, Tangaroa looked at the dry land his brother had won and chose the other half of creation: he went down into the ocean, and took it for his own. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1; Smith, The Lore of the Whare-wānanga.) The myth reads the coastline as a family wound: the sea is not the land's opposite but its brother, still angry.

myths.title: The Children Who Split in Two
myths.text: Not all the brothers accepted the separation. Tāwhirimātea, the wind, remained with his father in the sky and made war on the others, and Tangaroa's domain was his first battlefield: the sea boiled under the storm. In the rout, Tangaroa's grandchildren — the children of his son Punga — split forever. Ikatere, father of the fish, fled into the deep and cried 'swim, my children'; Tū-te-wehiwehi, father of the reptiles, scrambled ashore into Tāne's forests and cried 'hide, my children.' Hence the hostility the myth sees everywhere along the tideline: fish devour the lizards cast into the sea, and the sea never forgives the land. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) What looks like natural enmity is re-read as a family separated under fire — every fish a refugee, every lizard a deserter's child.

myths.title: Hine-moana, Mother of All That Swim
myths.text: In the traditions recorded by Elsdon Best, Tangaroa's wife is Hine-moana, 'ocean woman' — not a separate power but the sea itself, personified as the mother of the fish tribes. Every species is their child, which is why the fisherman addresses the sea as kin, and why the first fish of a catch was laid back into the water: a family does not eat its greeting. The canoes that crossed Hine-moana to reach Aotearoa were themselves spoken of as her children, and the rituals of launching, fishing, and beaching observed her tapu; even the nets and lines were named and placated. (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology; Best, The Māori as He Was.) The theology is ecological before the word existed: the ocean is not a resource but a marriage, and the catch is a relative arriving for dinner.

myths.title: The Same God in Other Islands
myths.text: Travel west and Tangaroa grows greater. In Tahiti the name becomes Ta'aroa, the self-existent creator from whose body the world was hatched (Henry, Ancient Tahiti). In Tonga and Samoa it is Tangaloa, the supreme god whose messenger, the plover Tuli, dove to the sea-bottom and brought up the sand of the first islands (Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology). In Hawai'i it is Kanaloa, companion of Kāne in the company of gods who made the first man, and lord of the ocean's dark deep (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology). The Māori sea-god is thus the eastern branch of the oldest divine name in Polynesia — which is why the nineteenth-century comparatists made him their first case study. One proto-god, four biographies: the triangle itself emerges as a single story told in dialects.

lore.syncretism: Tangaroa's syncretic career runs in two directions. Westward, in Tonga and Samoa, his name — Tangaloa — remained the supreme creator's, and Samoan Christians long prayed to a God they still sometimes called Tangaloa, a continuity the missionaries alternately welcomed and fought. Eastward, the Māori had already demoted him: from creator of the cosmos to lord of one domain, a brother among brothers, because the separation cycle re-hierarchized the gods around the family drama. In modern Aotearoa the name rides the cultural renaissance: Tangaroa appears in carving, kapa haka, and marine policy as the person of the moana, the sea that feeds and must be fed. The Treaty of Waitangi fisheries settlements of the 1980s and 90s, and the doctrine of kaitiakitanga over the marine estate, gave him a legal afterlife: his name is now cited wherever the sea is spoken of as an ancestor rather than a commodity.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tangaroa remains the most-seen of the Māori gods — in every coastal marae's imagery, in the school-taught separation cycle, and in the everyday word moana for the sea. Fishermen still speak of him half-jokingly and not entirely jokingly; the Māori fisheries claim and its settlement wrote his descendants' relationship with the sea into law. In Hawai'i, where his form is Kanaloa, the modern voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sails by the same star-compass the old navigators read — the sea-god's ancient craft, relaunched. Across the Pacific the name survives in hundreds of personal names, in ships, in the naming of research vessels, and in the quiet conviction of island peoples that the ocean is not empty water but occupied country.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Tangaroa is the sea as a relative — the most radical idea in the Māori cosmos. A god who is a brother, a domain that is a marriage, a catch that is a visit: the whole grammar of the ocean is familial, and the modern world's grammar of the ocean is exactly the opposite. When Māori negotiators in the 1980s and 90s said the sea is an ancestor, they were not inventing an environmentalism of convenience; they were quoting him. The name Tangaroa carries a complete theory of the deep: that the largest thing on the planet is a person with children, a temper, and a claim on our manners.

There is tragedy folded into the name as well. He is the brother who lost — who left rather than accept the new world, and whose children still flee one another at the water's edge. The tide that has run between brothers for all these generations is the one argument nobody has won: the land says the fish are food, the sea says the fish are family, and every meal from the ocean is a negotiation between the two.

sources.name: Orbell, Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend

lore.archaeology: No temple of Tangaroa survives, and Māori religion built none — but his archaeology is the archaeology of the sea. Coastal middens record the fisheries his priests regulated; the bone and shell of his children, stacked in heaps over centuries, are the oldest testimony to the relationship. Fish-hooks (matau) of bone, stone, and shell, many of superb workmanship, turn up wherever Māori camped on a coast; the great shank-hooks for snapper are functional sculpture. Rock shelters in the South Island preserve fish imagery read as ancestral. The canoe itself — the waka of the great voyages, surviving in fragments, adzes, and drilled hull-plugs — is his true monument: a technology of family visits.
